summary: Describes a protocol for registering and managing second-level domain names and their associated name servers, in both generic and country-code top-level domains. This is the Registry Registrar Protocol, version 1.1.0, as used by NSI. It is an informational memo.

eli5.summary: When you buy a web name, a shop must tell the main name office about it. This is the form and set of steps that shop used to do so.

questions: how do registrars register domain names
how domains are managed in the registry
subtitle: How registrars tell the DNS registry about new domains and name servers.

tldr.problem: When a registrar sells a domain name, they must tell the registry's database. The registry and registrar need a standard way to communicate about registering, renewing, modifying and transferring domains and their name servers.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2832 defines RRP (Registry Registrar Protocol), a text-based protocol over SSL/TLS where registrars send commands like ADD, CHECK, MOD, and RENEW to a registry server to manage domain and name server records.
tldr.outcome: Registrars can now automatically manage domain operations with a single registry via a standard protocol. RRP was used in the Shared Registration System. It was updated by RFC 3632.

today: RFC 2832 is an Informational memo from May 2000 documenting the NSI Registry Registrar Protocol as it was deployed. It was updated by RFC 3632.

sections.title: Domain Registration and Registrars
sections.content:
RFC 2832 describes the NSI Registry Registrar Protocol (RRP) version 1.1.0, a TCP-based text protocol for managing domain names and name servers. It enables multiple registrars to register and manage domains in Top Level Domains (TLDs) like .com, .org and country-code TLDs.

Internet domain registration involves three parties: the registrant (the person buying the domain), the registrar (the company selling it), and the registry (the authoritative database of all domains in that TLD). RRP is the protocol that the registrar and registry use to communicate—not the registrant. A registrar can use RRP to register, renew, update, check, and transfer domains and to manage name servers.
sections.eli5: Three people are involved: you (wanting a domain), the domain shop, and the registry office that keeps all the records. RRP is how the shop talks to the registry office.

sections.title: Security and Authentication
sections.content:
Every RRP connection MUST use SSL v3.0 (or the compatible TLS protocol) for privacy. Both the registrar client and the registry server are authenticated using digital certificates from a certification authority. In addition, the registrar must authenticate with a username and password at the start of each RRP session using the SESSION command.

The protocol enforces authorization rules: only the current registrar of a domain can renew it, update its name servers, or cancel it. Any registrar can request to transfer a domain from another registrar, but the current registrar must approve the transfer. Name servers can only be managed by their registrar.
sections.eli5: The conversation is encrypted so nobody can eavesdrop. Both sides prove who they are, and each registrar can only change their own domains.

sections.title: Connection States and Commands
sections.content:
An RRP session moves through states: first it waits for a client to authenticate, then it waits for commands, executes them, and finally disconnects. The server sends a banner when a client connects, confirming the connection is open.

Registrars send commands like ADD (to register a domain or name server), CHECK (to see if a domain is available), MOD (to update a domain), DEL (to delete a domain), RENEW (to extend registration), and TRANSFER (to move a domain to a new registrar). Every command is sent as text lines ending with carriage-return line-feed, and each command ends with a dot on its own line.
sections.eli5: The registrar sends typed commands, like 'add example.com' or 'check available-name.com', and the registry answers with success or an error code.

sections.title: Request and Response Format
sections.content:
An RRP request consists of a command name, entity data (attribute-value pairs), command options, and an end-of-command dot. For example, an ADD command to register a domain includes the command name, the entity type (Domain), the domain name, optional name servers, and a registration period.

An RRP response starts with a three-digit response code (like 200 for success) followed by a description, then zero or more attribute-value pairs with the result (such as the registration expiration date), and ends with a dot. Error codes indicate problems: for example, 211 means the domain name is not available (already taken).
sections.eli5: Requests and answers are plain text: the registrar says 'add domain:example.com' and the registry responds '200 Command completed successfully' with the expiration date.

sections.title: Domains, Name Servers and Status
sections.content:
The registry stores two main entities: domains (with name, expiration date, registrar, and status) and name servers (with name, IP addresses, and registrar). When registering a domain, the registrar can specify up to 13 name servers that must already be registered. Name servers are implicitly transferred when their parent domain is transferred to another registrar.

Domains have status values such as ACTIVE. A domain cannot be deleted if it has child name servers hosting other domains, and a name server cannot be deleted if it is hosting domains. This protection prevents orphaning domains when infrastructure is removed.
sections.eli5: Domains have names and expiration dates; name servers have names and IP addresses. Deleting things is blocked if it would break other domains.

sections.title: Idempotency and Error Recovery
sections.content:
All RRP commands are idempotent: executing a command once has the same effect as executing it multiple times. This is crucial for reliability. If a registrar sends a command and does not receive the response before a timeout, it can safely resend the command without worrying that it will be executed twice.

The protocol uses an "all or nothing" rule: if a command fails, the system stays in the same state it was before the command was attempted. Commands are processed in sequence, and the client should wait for a response before sending the next command to keep the connection in sync with the server.
sections.eli5: If your command times out, you can send it again without breaking things. The server either completes the whole command or does nothing.
